title: By whose grace
hook: jih prasaad: by whose grace you eat fine foods and wear fine clothes, remember Him

segments.voice: Yesterday, saranaagatee: five thieves, and a request for grace. Your line was grace clears the house. Today, that word grace becomes a drumbeat. Day four hundred fifty-nine.

Jih prasaad. Jih prasaad. Jih prasaad. Read ashtpadi six aloud and those two words come round again and again, at the start of line after line, like a drum keeping time under a song. By whose grace. By whose grace. By whose grace. Each time, a different gift follows. And the gifts in the first stanza are surprisingly ordinary for a sacred text. Not visions. Not miracles. Dinner. Perfume. A comfortable house. A good shirt. Things used every day without a second thought.
screen: `JIH PRASAAD, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `A DRUM UNDER THE SONG.` → `DINNER, PERFUME, A GOOD SHIRT.`

segments.voice: Jih means by whom, by whose. Prasaad, you met yesterday: grace, a gift freely given. In the gurdwara, the sweet offering given into cupped hands at the end of a service is called karah prashad, and today's word can be heard in its name. So jih prasaad: by whose free gift. The first stanza goes like this. By whose grace you eat the thirty-six delicacies, a phrase read as every kind of fine food, keep that Master in your mind. By whose grace you put fragrance on your body, remembering Him you reach the highest state. By whose grace you live in a house of comfort, meditate on Him always. And the next stanza picks up the clothes: by whose grace you wear silks and fine cloth, why abandon Him and cling to another? Notice the pattern. Every line has two halves. The first half is a gift you can taste, smell, touch. The second half is a turning: remember, keep in mind, don't forget. Guru Arjan doesn't ask anyone to give up the meal or the shirt. He asks for the meal to become a reminder. The food is real; it's where your attention goes next that the stanza cares about. It's the same move as the ten things, made smaller and more frequent. Not once a year at a feast. Every time you sit down to eat.
screen: `JIH: BY WHOSE. PRASAAD: FREE GIFT.` · `THE THIRTY-SIX DELICACIES.` · `EACH GIFT, THEN A TURNING.` · `THE MEAL BECOMES A REMINDER.` · then, large: `BY HIS GRACE, THIS MEAL.`

segments.voice: The practice is for your next meal: before you eat, pause and thank grace. For now, rehearse it. Picture the next thing you'll eat, a plate, a sandwich, a cup of tea. See where it came from: a field, a farmer, a truck, a shop, someone's hands. Then hear the drumbeat: jih prasaad, by whose grace. If you pray, let that be your thanks. If you don't, let it be a moment of noticing that none of it began with you. Breathe in: the meal. Breathe out: by whose grace. The bell holds the time.
Jih prasaad. By whose grace: the refrain of ashtpadi six, set before every ordinary gift.
Your line: by his grace, this meal. Before each meal today, even a snack, say the line once, silently, before the first bite. Day four hundred fifty-nine.

screen: `DAY 459 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BY WHOSE GRACE, THE BODY.`

howItsDone: Many Sikhs remember Waheguru before eating, and in the gurdwara karah prashad is received in cupped hands as a gift of grace; ashtpadi six's 'jih prasaad' refrain is read as part of Sukhmani Sahib.

original.note: Gurmukhi: jih prasaad, by whose grace; the refrain of Sukhmani's sixth ashtpadi.

trapdoor: what you thought: grace is for big moments.
what it means: in ashtpadi six it's set before dinner, perfume, a house and a shirt.
what a scholar hears: 'chhateeh amrit' (thirty-six nectars) is read as every kind of fine dish; the gurdwara's karah prashad carries the same word for a gift of grace.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
